abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) has emerged as a significant long-term complication in cancer survivors, particularly those undergoing chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or targeted therapies. Despite advances in treatment, CRCI affects patients' quality of life, impacting their daily functioning, work capacity, and psychological well-being. In recent years, research has focused on identifying predictive factors for CRCI and developing risk prediction models to facilitate early intervention. This review summarizes the latest progress in CRCI risk prediction models, including traditional statistical approaches such as logistic regression and advanced machine learning techniques. While machine learning models demonstrate superior predictive performance, limitations such as data availability and model interpretability remain. Additionally, the review highlights key risk factors—such as age, cancer type, and treatment modalities—and evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of various predictive models in terms of accuracy, generalizability, and clinical applicability. Finally, this paper discusses the challenges in validating these models across diverse populations and the need for further research to enhance model reliability and personalization of interventions.

sec.p: Keywords: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI), Risk prediction models, Machine learning, Logistic regression
Received 2024 Dec 12; Accepted 2025 Feb 5; Issue date 2025.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, cancer has emerged as a major public health challenge worldwide, becoming the leading cause of increased mortality rates globally. According to the 2024 Global Cancer Statistics released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), there were 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer-related deaths globally in 2022 [1]. Data indicate that in China alone, over 2 million cancer-related deaths occurred in 2020, representing a 21.6% increase compared to 2005 [2]. Lung, breast, and colorectal cancers are among the most prevalent types [3]. Although early screening, advanced treatment approaches, and increased national healthcare expenditures have gradually extended the survival time of cancer patients—with the five-year relative survival rate rising from 30.9% to 40.5% [4]—the extended survival period has brought greater attention to long-term health issues, such as cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI).

CRCI is a common and complex complication that typically arises in patients who have undergone cancer treatments, particularly those who have received chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or targeted therapies. It is characterized by declines in cognitive function, including memory impairment, difficulties in concentration, and deficits in executive function [5]. Research indicates that during and after treatment, the incidence of CRCI can reach up to 70% in patients with non-central nervous system cancers [6], and approximately 25% of survivors may continue to experience CRCI up to 20 years after completing their treatment [7]. This cognitive impairment not only significantly affects patients' daily activities and work capacity but can also further impact their psychological well-being, social functioning, and overall quality of life [8]. Although the pathogenesis of CRCI remains incompletely understood, studies have highlighted several contributing factors, including cancer type, treatment modalities, patient age, and psychological status. Additionally, the symptoms of CRCI may persist for months or even years, making early identification and effective risk prediction clinically significant.

Given the long-term health implications of CRCI for cancer survivors, there has been a growing focus on identifying its risk factors and developing risk prediction models in recent years. This review aims to summarize the progress in research on the risk factors for CRCI and related risk prediction models, analyzing the methodologies used for model development, their predictive performance, and their potential applications and limitations in clinical practice. Through a systematic review, this paper seeks to provide a reference for the early detection and intervention of CRCI, as well as to lay the groundwork for optimizing prediction models and developing personalized therapeutic strategies in the future.

sec.title: Predictive factors
sec.p: The mechanisms underlying CRCI are complex and multifaceted, involving a variety of factors. The multifactorial model of cancer-related cognitive impairment (MMCRCI) offers a systematic framework to comprehensively understand the origins of cognitive dysfunction in cancer patients [9]. This model is based on the premise that cognitive impairment is not driven by a single factor but rather results from the interaction of social, individual, treatment-related, and symptomatic influences. The following discussion explores CRCI through four primary dimensions: social determinants of health, patient-specific factors, treatment-related factors, and co-occurring symptoms.

sec.title: Social determinants of health
sec.p: Social determinants of health encompass the external environments and social conditions that influence individual health, and these factors significantly affect cognitive function in cancer patients. Studies indicate that cancer patients from low-income families are at a higher risk for cognitive impairment. Financial stress can exacerbate psychological burdens, thereby affecting cognitive processes [10]. Individuals with higher levels of education tend to have greater cognitive reserve, which enables them to better resist declines in cognitive function. Conversely, those with lower educational attainment may have reduced resilience against cognitive impairments [11]. Prolonged exposure to high-stress occupations or living conditions can also heighten vulnerability to cognitive decline [12]. The stress response triggered by a cancer diagnosis and its treatment can amplify pre-existing life stresses, further exacerbating cognitive symptoms. Moreover, social support and interpersonal relationships are crucial in alleviating psychological stress in cancer patients; those lacking social support are at greater risk for cognitive decline [13].

sec.title: Patient-specific factors
sec.p: Individual patient characteristics also play a critical role in the development of CRCI. Differences in physiological and psychological traits can make certain patients more susceptible to cognitive dysfunction. For example, older patients tend to experience faster declines in cognitive function after cancer treatment due to age-related brain degeneration and reduced tolerance to therapies like chemotherapy [14]. Research has also suggested that female patients may be more prone to cognitive declines post-treatment, possibly due to differences in neurobiological responses to stress [15]. Personality traits, such as high levels of anxiety and depressive tendencies, are directly associated with increased risks of cognitive impairment. Additionally, the overall physical condition of patients can impact cognitive outcomes; those with poorer functional status are more vulnerable to cognitive deficits when facing the physiological and psychological challenges of treatment.

sec.title: Treatment-related factors
sec.p: The cognitive function of cancer patients is directly influenced by treatment modalities, particularly conventional therapies like chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Decreased hemoglobin levels during chemotherapy are closely associated with cognitive decline. Lower hemoglobin can result in inadequate oxygen supply to the brain, negatively affecting cognitive abilities. Abnormal white blood cell counts can also impact neurocognitive function, especially when the immune system is compromised, increasing the likelihood of cognitive issues. The type, dosage, and duration of chemotherapy drugs can differentially affect cognitive function [14]. Some drugs, such as cyclophosphamide and methotrexate, are considered high risk for inducing cognitive impairment. Medications used to manage nausea during chemotherapy, particularly certain sedatives, may also contribute to cognitive side effects.

sec.title: Co-occurring symptoms
sec.p: Cancer patients often experience a range of symptoms during treatment that can exacerbate or indirectly contribute to cognitive decline. Anxiety is strongly correlated with cognitive impairment, with higher anxiety levels often leading to decreased attention and memory [16]. Depression, a common mood disorder, is significantly associated with CRCI, not only directly impairing cognitive function but also exacerbating the side effects of cancer treatments [17]. Poor sleep quality is prevalent among cancer patients, and sleep disturbances can hinder the brain's normal recovery processes, leading to cognitive decline [18]. Pain can divert patients' focus and attention, and the long-term use of analgesics for pain management can further impair cognitive function.

sec.title: Predictive models
sec.p: Using the search strategy (("Neoplasms"[Mesh] OR cancer[Title/Abstract] OR cancers[Title/Abstract] OR tumor[Title/Abstract] OR tumour[Title/Abstract] OR oncology[Title/Abstract]) AND ("Cognitive Dysfunction"[Mesh] OR "Cognitive Impairment"[Title/Abstract] OR "Cancer-related cognitive impairment"[Title/Abstract] OR CRCI[Title/Abstract] OR "chemo brain"[Title/Abstract] OR "chemo fog"[Title/Abstract]) AND ("Risk Assessment"[Mesh] OR "Prediction Model"[Title/Abstract] OR "Risk Prediction"[Title/Abstract] OR "Risk Factors"[Title/Abstract] OR "Prognostic Model"[Title/Abstract] OR "Prediction tool"[Title/Abstract])), we systematically searched the National Library of Medicine database (PubMed), the Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and the Web of Science for literature related to risk prediction models for cognitive impairment in cancer patients. The search combined MeSH terms with free-text keywords. In addition, manual searches and reference tracking were conducted to supplement the identified literature. The search covered publications from the inception of the databases to August 2024, and only English-language studies were included.
Inclusion Criteria:

list-item.p: Study types: Cohort studies, case–control studies, and cross-sectional studies;
Study population: Patients diagnosed with cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI);

Study content:i.
Research focused on developing or validating risk prediction models for CRCI;ii.
Detailed descriptions of the modeling process and statistical methods used;iii.
For duplicate publications, the most recent or the study with the largest sample size was included.

sec.p: Exclusion Criteria:

list-item.p: Studies that did not provide criteria for the diagnosis of cognitive impairment;
Research that analyzed risk factors but did not develop a risk prediction model;
Conference abstracts, academic theses, or other unpublished documents;
Review articles, commentaries, or news reports;
Studies where full text was unavailable or with incomplete abstract information;
Publications in languages other than Chinese or English.

sec.p: Two independent researchers screened the literature and extracted data, including information such as researchers, year(s), sample size, model validation methods, predictive factors, modeling methods, and AUC statistics. Cross-checking was performed, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third party.

sec.title: Statistical models
sec.p: The logistic regression model, as a traditional statistical prediction method, has several advantages. It is simple and easy to understand, and it allows for a clear explanation of the impact of various risk factors on CRCI, particularly through the calculation of odds ratios to assess the role of each factor. Additionally, logistic regression is well suited for binary classification problems (e.g., the presence or absence of cognitive impairment) and can provide stable predictive results even with smaller sample sizes. However, this method also has some limitations. First, it assumes a linear relationship between the independent variables and the outcome, making it less effective in handling nonlinear or complex interaction effects. Second, logistic regression is sensitive to multicollinearity and outliers, which may lead to model instability. Moreover, when the model includes a large number of irrelevant variables, its predictive performance may decline. Therefore, while logistic regression has practical utility in CRCI risk prediction, more complex datasets may require the integration of other methods to improve predictive accuracy.

Zhou and colleagues employed a cross-sectional design anchored in a symptom science model to predict the risk of cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) among breast cancer patients. Drawing from a cohort of 515 individuals, they developed a predictive model using multivariate logistic regression. To ensure reliability, they conducted internal validation via the bootstrap resampling method (1,000 iterations). Significant predictive factors identified included the patient's place of residence, education level, chemotherapy regimen, benefit finding, post-traumatic growth, anxiety, fear of cancer progression, and fasting blood glucose levels. Their final nomogram yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.955 (95% CI 0.939–0.971), showcasing excellent discriminatory power and solid calibration. The model’s high predictive accuracy and ability to pinpoint high-risk patients effectively are notable strengths. However, its cross-sectional nature limits causal inference, and the absence of external validation detracts from its broader applicability [19].

In a retrospective analysis, Wang and his team focused on predicting postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) in elderly gastric cancer patients. With a sample size of 687, they employed multivariate logistic regression to build their model and validated its performance using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Noteworthy predictors included preoperative ASA classification, patient age, surgery duration, preoperative PG-SGA score, hemoglobin levels, the intraoperative administration of dexmedetomidine, and the depth of anesthesia. The resulting model demonstrated an AUC of 0.820 (95% CI 0.742–0.899), indicating good discriminatory ability and calibration. The model’s strength lies in its potential to identify high-risk individuals at an early stage, paving the way for timely intervention. Yet, limitations such as the relatively small sample size and absence of external validation cast doubt on its generalizability [20].

Genan and colleagues pursued a prospective longitudinal study to explore the risk factors for cognitive impairment among cancer patients receiving hospice care. Their sample of 1,568 patients underwent cognitive assessments using a simplified version of the mini-mental state examination (MMSE), with follow-ups conducted 4 to 16 weeks later. The research team utilized multivariate logistic regression to create their predictive model, managing missing data with multiple imputation techniques. The findings highlighted that a low Karnofsky performance status (≤ 70%) was an independent predictor of cognitive impairment (OR = 1.6, 95% CI 1.0–2.5), while breast cancer patients exhibited a lower risk (OR = 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.7). Notably, 24% of patients developed cognitive impairment during follow-up, although 11.6% showed improvement. The model excels at identifying high-risk patients early on; however, the high dropout rate during follow-up and insufficient detail regarding medication use present significant limitations [21].

In another multicenter cross-sectional study, Liu and his team evaluated CRCI risk among breast cancer patients. They gathered data from 741 participants and applied LASSO regression to identify significant variables, followed by the construction of a logistic regression model. Key factors included education level, frequency of physical activity, number of chemotherapy cycles, and fatigue levels. The model’s performance, validated through fivefold cross-validation, achieved an AUC of 0.882, reflecting strong discriminatory ability. The model's major advantage lies in its ability to swiftly assess CRCI risk using clinical data, thus supporting early intervention. However, similar to other cross-sectional studies, it faces limitations in establishing causal relationships and lacks validation using external datasets [22].

Amir and his team conducted a multicenter cross-sectional analysis to investigate the long-term disease burden among intracranial meningioma patients, with a specific focus on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and neurocognitive function predictors. Based on a sample of 190 patients, they employed multivariate logistic regression to develop their predictive model, evaluating its performance using the C-statistic. Key predictors encompassed age, education level, complications, reoperations, radiotherapy, tumor size, and time since diagnosis. The HRQoL model achieved an AUC of 0.72 (95% CI 0.63–0.80), while the neurocognitive function model produced an AUC of 0.78 (95% CI 0.70–0.85), indicating moderate to good discriminatory power. The strength of these models lies in their capacity to identify patients at high risk for long-term disease burden, facilitating personalized interventions. However, the use of only internal validation and the absence of external validation raise concerns about their broader applicability [23].

Sayo and colleagues undertook a longitudinal observational study to explore cognitive impairment risk in elderly patients with hematologic malignancies undergoing initial chemotherapy. Based on a sample of 145 patients, clinical indicators of cognitive impairment were identified using multivariate logistic regression, with model performance evaluated through ROC curve analysis. Predictive factors included lower educational attainment, diminished capacity for instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), and subjective perceptions of memory difficulties. The model attained an AUC of 0.81, demonstrating good predictive power for identifying high-risk patients. Its ability to flag individuals for early intervention is a key strength, though the small sample size and brief follow-up period limit the model’s capacity to assess the long-term effects of chemotherapy on cognitive function [24].

There are several significant limitations in studies developing CRCI prediction models based on logistic regression. First, insufficient sample size can lead to the problem of overfitting, where the model performs well on the training data but has poor generalizability to new data. This issue is particularly common in CRCI research, as sample collection may be restricted to specific clinical settings or patient populations. This limitation reduces the model's applicability to a broader range of cancer patients. Second, CRCI studies often face the challenge of missing data, yet lack effective methods to address this issue. For instance, more advanced techniques like multiple imputation should be used to avoid the biases introduced by deleting or simply filling in missing data, which could compromise the model’s accuracy. Third, many studies convert continuous variables into binary categories. While this simplification may make the model easier to interpret, it results in a loss of rich information contained in the original data, thereby weakening the model’s ability to accurately predict CRCI risk. Additionally, many CRCI prediction models lack the use of calibration curves in performance evaluation. Although metrics like AUC can assess a model's discriminatory ability, calibration curves are better suited to evaluate the match between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes, providing a more comprehensive validation of the model's accuracy. Finally, the absence of external validation is a major drawback in CRCI prediction model research. While internal validation methods (e.g., cross-validation or bootstrap resampling) provide an initial assessment, without validation on different populations or external datasets, the model’s generalizability and applicability to diverse cancer patient groups are limited, hindering its broader clinical use.

sec.title: Machine learning models
sec.p: Machine learning (ML) has become an important tool in CRCI risk prediction studies due to its ability to handle high-dimensional data, complex variable relationships, and nonlinear pattern recognition. Traditional statistical models rely on predefined assumptions about variable relationships, whereas machine learning takes a data-driven approach, automatically learning features and patterns from complex clinical, genomic, and imaging data, thereby improving predictive accuracy and robustness.

Zhu and colleagues undertook a cross-sectional analysis aiming to evaluate the risk of cognitive impairment in patients with advanced cancer while contrasting the effectiveness of various predictive models. This study involved a cohort of 494 advanced cancer patients, from whom significant clinical indicators were initially identified through univariate analysis. A subsequent multivariate analysis employed two distinct models: an artificial neural network (ANN) model, specifically a multilayer perceptron, and a logistic regression model. To gauge the models' predictive power, the area under the ROC curve (AUC) was utilized. Findings highlighted that factors such as cancer duration, anxiety, and age were critical risk elements. Notably, the ANN model surpassed the logistic regression model, demonstrating superior accuracy, sensitivity, and an AUC of 0.910. These results suggest that the ANN model may offer enhanced potential for predicting cognitive impairment in advanced cancer patients, thereby supporting early clinical interventions. Nevertheless, the study's limitations, including its single-region scope, limited sample diversity, and cross-sectional design, constrain its ability to infer causality effectively [25].

In another investigation, Xu and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study focused on predicting the likelihood of postoperative chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) among patients undergoing colorectal cancer stoma surgery. The research comprised 108 participants, and a random forest algorithm was employed for feature selection. The final predictive model was constructed using the support vector machine-recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE) method. Key determinants identified were age, exercise intensity, body mass index (BMI), comorbidities, and cancer-related anemia (CRA). The model's robustness was evaluated using ROC curves, where the SVM-RFE model achieved a remarkable AUC of 0.909, underscoring its strong predictive capabilities. One of the model's primary strengths lies in its capacity to accurately isolate influential factors associated with CRCI. However, challenges such as the relatively small sample size and the absence of external dataset validation raise concerns about its broader applicability [26].

Similarly, Noha and colleagues pursued a prospective longitudinal study to assess the risk of cognitive decline in patients with hematologic malignancies post blood or marrow transplantation (BMT). This study involved 277 participants, with the team leveraging an Elastic-Net regression method to develop a predictive model that integrated genetic, clinical, and demographic factors. The model's performance was measured using AUC, with further validation performed in an independent cohort of BMT survivors. Significant predictors included age, gender, total body irradiation (TBI), baseline cognitive reserve, and genes associated with DNA repair and the blood–brain barrier. The integrated model, enriched with genetic data, yielded an AUC of 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93) in the discovery cohort, while in the validation cohort, it achieved an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66–0.76), outperforming models relying solely on clinical and demographic information. Despite its enhanced predictive precision, the reliance on genetic factors and variability in cognitive assessment methods across cohorts present challenges to the model's generalizability [27].

Although machine learning methods have shown great potential in CRCI prediction models, several limitations remain. First, machine learning models typically require large datasets to ensure stability and accuracy. However, in clinical settings—particularly when focusing on specific conditions such as CRCI—acquiring sufficiently large sample sizes is often challenging. Insufficient sample sizes not only limit the training effectiveness of the model but also increase the risk of overfitting, which can cause the model to perform poorly on new data. Second, the lack of interpretability in machine learning models is a significant challenge in current research. Unlike logistic regression models, machine learning models such as deep learning and random forests, while excelling in predictive performance, are often considered “black box” models. This makes it difficult to clearly explain the specific impact of each variable on CRCI. In clinical practice, this is particularly crucial, as both doctors and patients typically need to understand the model's rationale in order to trust and accept the predictive results (Table 1).

sec.title: Comparison of statistical models and machine learning models
sec.p: Traditional statistical models, such as logistic regression, are widely used in CRCI risk prediction due to their simplicity and interpretability. Logistic regression provides clear explanations of the impact of individual risk factors through odds ratios, making it easier for clinicians to understand and apply [28]. For example, Zhou et al.'s logistic regression model for CRCI prediction achieved a high AUC (0.955) [19], demonstrating robust discriminative ability while maintaining interpretability. However, statistical models have limitations, such as assuming linear relationships between variables and outcomes, which may oversimplify the complex interplay of factors in CRCI. Additionally, their performance diminishes in the presence of high-dimensional data or nonlinear interactions, both of which are common in CRCI datasets. Moreover, they are sensitive to multicollinearity, outliers, and missing data, which may lead to biased results [29].

In contrast, ML models excel in handling large, high-dimensional datasets with complex nonlinear relationships. Techniques such as artificial neural networks (ANNs), random forests, and support vector machines (SVMs) have demonstrated superior predictive accuracy in CRCI studies. For instance, Zhu et al. reported that an ANN model outperformed logistic regression, achieving an AUC of 0.910 versus 0.782 [25]. These models automatically learn patterns from data, offering higher flexibility and adaptability. However, their primary limitation is the “black box” nature, which obscures the contributions of individual variables and reduces interpretability [30]. This lack of transparency can hinder clinical adoption, where understanding a model's rationale is vital for gaining trust from both clinicians and patients. Additionally, ML models often require large datasets to avoid overfitting and ensure generalizability, a challenge in CRCI research due to the relatively small sample sizes [31].

For CRCI risk prediction, statistical models are beneficial when the goal is to identify and quantify individual risk factors for cognitive impairment. They are particularly useful in scenarios with limited datasets or when a straightforward, interpretable model is needed. On the other hand, ML models are advantageous when dealing with complex, multifactorial datasets that integrate clinical, genetic, and psychosocial variables. They offer higher predictive power, especially in identifying subtle interactions between predictors, but require careful consideration of data availability, preprocessing, and model validation to ensure reliability.

sec.title: The risk of bias in predictive models
sec.p: The PROBAST results [32] indicate that all nine included studies had a high risk of bias, with the majority of biases concentrated in the analysis domain (Table 2). The main issues included the following six aspects: (1) One study had a severely underpowered sample for modeling, with fewer than 20 events per variable [26]; (2) one study transformed continuous variables into two or more categories based on cutoff values [27]; (3) five studies did not report how missing data were handled [19, 20, 23, 26, 27], and one study directly excluded missing data [21]; (4) four studies did not report whether internal validation was performed [20, 21, 23, 24], indicating a lack of model performance evaluation; (5) four studies [19, 20, 25, 26] selected predictive factors based on univariate analysis; and (6) five studies [20, 21, 23, 25, 27] did not report whether they assessed model calibration. In terms of model applicability, three studies were rated as having low applicability because the models were constructed using only elderly patients as study subjects [20, 24, 26].

sec.title: Bias in data collection and population representation
sec.p: Many CRCI prediction studies rely on datasets that are limited in diversity, often focusing on specific cancer types (e.g., breast cancer) or demographic groups. For instance, older patients or those undergoing specific therapies are commonly overrepresented, while younger patients or those receiving non-chemotherapy treatments are underrepresented. This lack of diversity introduces selection bias, limiting the model's applicability across broader patient populations. Furthermore, studies often exclude patients with missing data or those lost to follow-up, resulting in attrition bias. Such exclusions may lead to an overestimation of the model's accuracy and reduce its real-world utility [33].

sec.title: Measurement and reporting bias
sec.p: CRCI is assessed using various cognitive tests and self-reported measures, which may not always be standardized across studies. Discrepancies in the instruments used for cognitive assessment introduce measurement bias, affecting the comparability of datasets and the robustness of predictive models [34]. Additionally, reliance on subjective measures, such as patient-reported symptoms, may lead to reporting bias, where psychological factors like anxiety or depression disproportionately influence reported outcomes.

sec.title: Modeling and methodological bias
sec.p: Several limitations in modeling methodologies contribute to bias in CRCI research, including overfitting due to small datasets with insufficient statistical power (e.g., using fewer than 10 events per variable in logistic regression), inadequate handling of missing data through simplistic methods instead of robust techniques like multiple imputation, and variable selection bias caused by reliance on univariate analysis, which can overlook critical interactions and artificially inflate model performance during validation [35].

sec.title: Bias in model validation
sec.p: Internal validation methods, such as cross-validation or bootstrap resampling, are commonly used but insufficient to ensure generalizability. Many CRCI studies lack external validation using independent datasets, which is critical for evaluating the model's performance in diverse populations. Without external validation, models are prone to validation bias, which inflates their apparent accuracy and clinical utility [36].

sec.title: Conclusion and summary
sec.p: Despite progress in developing CRCI prediction models, their clinical adoption remains limited due to several barriers. A lack of standardization and external validation on diverse datasets undermines confidence in their robustness and generalizability. Interpretability challenges, particularly with advanced machine learning models like ANNs and SVMs, hinder trust and usability in clinical settings due to their “black box” nature. Additionally, limited integration into clinical workflows, such as through electronic health record-compatible tools, restricts real-time application. While no models are currently in widespread use, promising examples like Zhou et al.’s nomogram highlight potential with further validation.

sec.title: Need for improvement in predictive models
sec.p: A key issue across many CRCI prediction models is the limited sample size, which increases the risk of overfitting and reduces the generalizability of the models to broader patient populations. Most studies have employed internal validation techniques like cross-validation, but few have been externally validated across diverse populations, limiting their clinical applicability. Furthermore, missing data remain a common problem, with many studies either failing to address it properly or relying on simple imputation methods that may introduce bias. More advanced techniques such as multiple imputation and handling continuous variables more effectively could enhance model performance.

Additionally, model calibration is often overlooked, even though it is critical for ensuring that predicted probabilities align well with actual outcomes. While many models achieve high discriminatory power, as indicated by AUC scores, calibration metrics provide a more nuanced understanding of the model’s accuracy in a clinical setting. Without this, predictive models may provide misleading probabilities of risk, diminishing their utility in practice.

sec.title: Analysis of predictive factors
sec.p: The factors identified as predictive of CRCI are multifaceted, spanning demographic, clinical, genetic, and psychosocial dimensions. Age, educational background, comorbidities, and specific cancer treatments (e.g., chemotherapy and radiotherapy) consistently emerge as key risk factors. More recent studies have incorporated genetic information, such as variations in DNA repair genes and blood–brain barrier function, which have been shown to significantly enhance model performance. However, the integration of genetic data into predictive models presents challenges due to the high cost and complexity of genomic testing, making it less accessible in routine clinical practice.

Additionally, psychosocial factors, such as anxiety, depression, and social support, play a critical role in the development of CRCI but are often underrepresented in predictive models. A more holistic approach that includes both biological and psychosocial factors is essential for improving the accuracy of CRCI prediction and tailoring interventions to individual patient needs.

sec.title: Clinical implications
sec.p: From a clinical perspective, the development of robust CRCI prediction models holds the potential to significantly improve patient outcomes. Early identification of high-risk individuals allows for timely interventions, such as cognitive training, lifestyle modifications, and psychological support, which could mitigate the impact of cognitive impairment on cancer survivors. Moreover, as cancer treatments continue to extend survival times, addressing the long-term cognitive side effects becomes an increasingly important aspect of survivorship care.

Despite the progress made, there is a pressing need for further research to refine these models and ensure their applicability across different cancer types and patient populations. This includes larger, multicenter studies to validate model performance, greater integration of genetic and psychosocial variables, and the adoption of advanced data handling techniques. Ultimately, improving the predictive accuracy and generalizability of CRCI models will enhance clinicians’ ability to provide personalized, proactive care to cancer patients, mitigating the cognitive burdens associated with cancer treatments.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Future research should prioritize the following areas:
External Validation Validation of existing models using larger and more diverse datasets is critical to improve the generalizability of CRCI prediction models across different populations.

Integration of Advanced Technologies The incorporation of machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, combined with larger genomic datasets, can further enhance model accuracy and uncover new predictive biomarkers.

Holistic Approach Future models should include a broader range of predictive factors, integrating genetic, biological, and psychosocial elements to provide a more comprehensive assessment of CRCI risk.

Clinical Implementation Developing user-friendly tools and platforms that can easily be integrated into clinical workflows will be essential for translating research findings into practical interventions.

The integration of electronic health records (EHRs) into CRCI research: The integration of electronic health records (EHRs) into cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) research offers transformative opportunities to advance prediction model development. EHRs provide a vast repository of real-world clinical data, encompassing demographic information, treatment histories, laboratory results, imaging data, and long-term outcomes. By leveraging such extensive datasets, researchers can enhance the statistical power and generalizability of CRCI prediction models, overcoming limitations such as small sample sizes and population homogeneity. The diversity captured within EHR datasets allows models to be applicable across different demographic groups and clinical settings, addressing one of the most pressing challenges in current CRCI prediction research.

In addition to broadening population representation, EHRs facilitate the discovery of novel predictive factors. Beyond traditional clinical variables, EHRs enable the inclusion of longitudinal data on comorbidities, medication use, and psychosocial influences, such as mental health conditions. With the aid of advanced analytics and machine learning, these datasets can uncover complex interactions and nonlinear relationships, potentially identifying new contributors to CRCI that were previously unrecognized. Furthermore, the longitudinal nature of EHR data supports long-term validation of prediction models, ensuring their reliability and durability in real-world scenarios.

EHRs also hold the promise of real-time integration into clinical workflows. Predictive models embedded within EHR systems can provide clinicians with instant CRCI risk assessments during patient visits, enabling timely identification of high-risk individuals and facilitating early interventions. This seamless integration aligns with the goals of personalized medicine and represents a crucial step toward improving patient outcomes. Moreover, by aggregating data from multiple institutions, EHR-based research reduces selection bias, enhances model applicability and ensures that the findings are reflective of diverse patient populations. Advanced EHR systems can also address common challenges, such as missing data, through integrated tools that improve the completeness and accuracy of datasets.

Despite these promising opportunities, challenges remain in harnessing EHRs for CRCI research. Variability in data entry practices and coding across institutions can limit the comparability of datasets, highlighting the need for standardized data collection frameworks like Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR). Ethical considerations, particularly regarding patient privacy and data security, also require careful attention to ensure compliance with data governance regulations. Finally, the computational demands of processing large EHR datasets necessitate significant investment in machine learning infrastructure and interdisciplinary collaboration between healthcare providers and data scientists.

In conclusion, while current predictive models for CRCI show promise, they remain a work in progress. With further refinement, these models have the potential to transform CRCI management, offering personalized, data-driven approaches that could substantially improve patient care and quality of life.
